clinicalPearls: A striking retinal vasculitis in which widespread perivascular sheathing gives the vessels a translucent 'frosted branch' appearance resembling frost on a tree
It is a clinical sign rather than a single disease and may be idiopathic or secondary to infection, autoimmune disease or lymphoma
The idiopathic form often affects otherwise healthy children and young adults with acute bilateral visual loss
Secondary causes include herpesviruses, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, syphilis and systemic vasculitis, which must be actively excluded
Vascular sheathing predominantly involves the veins but arteries may also be affected
The idiopathic form generally responds well to corticosteroids, whereas secondary forms need the underlying cause treated
reference.pathophysiology: Frosted branch angiitis reflects intense perivascular inflammation of the retinal vessels, thought in the idiopathic form to be an immune-mediated hypersensitivity response, sometimes following a viral illness. Dense inflammatory cuffing of the vessel walls produces the characteristic sheathing, with associated vascular leakage, macular oedema and, in severe cases, ischaemia. When secondary, the vasculitis is driven by direct infection or by a systemic inflammatory or neoplastic process affecting the retinal vasculature.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus or other autoimmune retinal vasculitis
additionalInvestigations: Fluorescein angiography to map leakage, occlusion and ischaemia
Infective screen including herpesviruses, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma and syphilis
Optical coherence tomography for macular oedema
Consideration of intraocular sampling if masquerade is suspected
redFlags: Evidence of an infective cause requiring specific therapy before steroids
Profound or progressive bilateral visual loss
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is often good in the idiopathic corticosteroid-responsive form, but outcomes in secondary disease depend on the underlying cause and on complications such as ischaemia and macular oedema.
pitfalls: Treating with corticosteroids before excluding infection
Assuming it is always idiopathic and missing lymphoma or systemic vasculitis
Overlooking the fellow eye in apparently unilateral cases
Failing to monitor for ischaemic complications
management: Systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay for the idiopathic immune-mediated form, to which it usually responds well

Directed treatment of any secondary cause, with antivirals for herpesviruses and cytomegalovirus, anti-toxoplasma therapy, or treatment of syphilis, and appropriate antimicrobial cover before immunosuppression when infection is possible
Immunosuppressive therapy for underlying systemic vasculitis or autoimmune disease, and treatment of lymphoma where a masquerade is identified
Management of macular oedema and monitoring for retinal ischaemia and neovascular complications
Fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography surveillance of vascular leakage, occlusion and macular oedema during treatment
Multidisciplinary input from uveitis specialists and physicians to identify and treat the underlying cause
Follow-up to taper corticosteroids and detect recurrence
